column11: Imports point inward, toward stability, and form no cycle, direct or through a chain of modules.
The inner layer declares, in its own words, the contracts it needs; the outer layer implements them.
The domain imports only itself and the shared kernel: no framework, no input or output, no vendor library, however pure.
Each layer, module and unit has one reason to change.
Every datum and every piece of state lives in one place; everything else reads it or derives from it.
A feature never imports another feature.
A module is reached from outside only through its surface, and the surface is curated: it offers what a caller may couple to and nothing else.
An external shape — a response, a row, a message, a file format — is mapped to the inner model at the edge, in both directions.
Input and output, network, storage, clock, randomness and processes live in adapters.
Concrete implementations are chosen and wired in one known place, the composition root.
Where one operation reads and another writes, the read path and the write path never import each other.
Code lives in the layer that owns its reason to change, beside its consumer when they share that reason, and lifts to the nearest common level only when a second consumer appears.
A value with distinct stages is a union keyed by its state, not a bag of optional fields and flags that allows combinations no stage has.
A caught error is handled, rethrown, or mapped to a typed error.
Every rule whose Check names a role is held by a tool of that role in the project's check, configured to fail on a violation.
A contract is shaped by the role that uses it: a reader sees only reads, a writer only writes, and no caller receives an operation it has no reason to call.
Input from outside the program — a request, a response, a file, the environment — is parsed once, at the edge, into a known type.
A new kind of thing — a vendor, a command, a format, a rule — is added as a new member and its registration, without editing the code that handles the other kinds.
Across bounded contexts, duplication is the default and sharing the exception.
A value object is built only through the function that checks its invariant, so a value that exists is valid.

Where the program owns the data it changes, every change goes through its aggregate's root, which keeps the aggregate consistent; an aggregate stays small, and a child with a life of its own becomes an aggregate referenced by identifier.
A program's source is laid out by concern in the folders of the top-level tree, and in no other top-level folder.
`root/` is imported only by entry files and by the delivery layer's own wiring.
No code imports an entrypoint.
`kernel/` imports only itself.
`libs/` imports no application code — no feature, `kernel/`, `shared/`, `contracts/`, `adapters/` or `root/` — and knows nothing of the repository that uses it.
`shared/` imports no feature and not `root/`.
A shared piece with business meaning goes to `kernel/`; one without goes to `shared/`; one that would make sense in any program goes to `libs/`.
Composition across features lives in the delivery unit that needs it, which assembles features through their surfaces.
A protocol two artifacts of one repository speak — the messages an embedded frame and its host exchange — lives in `shared/<protocol>/`, imported by both.
A file a tool produces carries `.gen` in its name or sits in a folder named `*.gen/`, and is never edited by hand; a change goes to its source, and the file is regenerated.
A feature is laid out as `domain/`, `adapters/<system>/` and `app/` with the role folders of the tree, and a surface at its root.

A data port is a repository per aggregate, one file per side: `repositories/queries/<aggregate>.repository` for reads and `repositories/commands/<aggregate>.repository` for writes, each declaring its operations' parameters and results.
A domain use-case exists only when its operation carries business logic.
A contract — a port, its parameters and results — imports no vendor, no adapter, no feature other than its own, and no other contract's internals.
An adapter imports its contracts, `kernel/` and `libs/`, and never a feature's application layer, the delivery layer or another adapter.
A feature that needs an answer from another declares a contract in its own words and receives an input built for it; composition implements the contract through the other feature's surface.
Outside a folder, a caller imports only its surface.
A layer folder — `domain/`, `app/`, `adapters/`, `src/`, `features/`, `libs/` — has no surface and is never an import target.
A surface re-exports by name what callers may use: no declaration, no logic, no re-export of everything.
A feature's surface offers its operations and its presentation — use-cases, binding units, entities, widgets — and never its mechanisms: repositories, mappers, wire types, cache keys.
A contract belongs to the feature that needs it.
An adapter implements, over one external system, every contract of its owner that system serves; it lives beside its contracts' owner.
An adapter receives its dependencies — the transport, the clients it speaks through — and is built by a factory function from them; it never imports a shared instance.
A port for an effect — clock, file system, processes, network — is a contract placed like any other, its real implementation is an adapter, and only a composition root chooses the real one.
A vendor client without application knowledge, and any pure project-agnostic helper, lives in `libs/<system>/`.
A delivery unit that serves one feature lives in that feature's `app/`, where the entry surface allows it; one that composes several lives in the delivery layer or in `composition/`.
A delivery unit — a screen, a command, a handler, a tool function — parses its input, calls a use-case or a binding unit, and presents the result.
A folder is named for its purpose, or by a role of the vocabulary of the project's active blocks.
A folder holds one purpose, said in one phrase without "and".
Files of one kind that arrive one at a time — one per vendor, command, rule or section — live in a folder named for the member in the plural, and nothing else lives there.
A file carries its role's suffix, whatever its folder: `entities/chat.entity`.
A YAML file ends in `.yaml`, never `.yml`.
A name says what a thing is for: intention-revealing, pronounceable, searchable, with no abbreviation that is not already a term of the domain and no noise word.
Names follow the business's own words, from the glossary of `PROJECT.md`: `cancelOrder`, not `updateRecord`.
One concept has one word across the program, and one word names one concept: not `fetch`, `load` and `get` for the same act.
No name is only an empty word — `data`, `result`, `temp`, `info`, `item`, `value`, `obj`, `arr`, `stuff`, `thing` — as a variable, a parameter or a destructured field.
A function is named by a concrete verb and its object, never an empty verb alone: `handle`, `process`, `manage`, `do`, `run`, `execute`, `get`, `set`, `update`.
A collection is named in the plural and one of its items in the singular, destructured names included.
An event is named for what happened, in the past tense: `OrderPlaced`, not `PlaceOrder`.
A domain name names the concept, never the vendor or the storage behind it: `UserRecord`, not `UserMongoDocument`.
A value with a unit carries the unit in its name: `timeoutMs`, `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS`, `sizeBytes`.
A file holds one semantic unit and is named after it; unrelated exports go to their own files.
A boolean variable, parameter or predicate starts with `is`, `has`, `can`, `should` or `did`.
Every argument past the first is named: the language's options record or keyword-only parameters.
A function does one thing, at one level of abstraction.
A function holds at most 100 lines, a file at most 500, and a function's cognitive complexity is at most 10.
Failure paths leave first, through guard clauses, so the main path stays at the top level of indentation.
A module hides much behind a small interface.
A function's output depends only on its input.
A longer, obvious form beats a terse, obscure one.
A comment states a constraint, a workaround or a decision the code cannot show.
Interface documentation is written only for a public interface whose use is not obvious from its names and types.
A to-do comment names its issue: `TODO(#<issue>)`.
Code is never commented out; it is deleted.
No unused file, dependency, export, parameter, variable or branch.
Shipped code writes no debug output and stops at no breakpoint; diagnostics go through the logging port.
Silencing a check — a lint rule, a type error, a mutant, a deliberately ignored error — carries its reason beside it.
Internal code spells absence with one value, which the language block names.
An expected failure is typed, carries a stable code `<MODULE>_<ENTITY>_<KIND>` and details that say what to do, and belongs to the contract that can fail.
A mapped error keeps its cause.
Defects travel to the boundary.
Only a transient failure — a timeout, a dropped connection, a rate limit — is retried, with backoff and a limit.
An error library gives every error a stable code, its cause and structured details, and a guard that recognises its errors by code.
A schema over a domain type or enum derives its values from it and is checked by type against what it produces.
A type guard checks every property of the type it claims.
An entity's identifier is a type of its own, branded by its entity, so an order's identifier cannot be passed where a user's is expected.
A type lives beside the unit whose signature introduces it, and every other unit imports it from there.
Values are immutable by default; a change makes a new value.
Clock, randomness, identifiers and the environment are reached through ports, never called directly from the logic.
One place reads the environment: `root/`, or the configuration provider a lower block names.
Asynchronous work is awaited, or detached on purpose with its failure handled.
Every call across a process boundary has a timeout and can be cancelled.
Concurrent work is started within a scope that waits for it, cancels it, and receives its failures; no task outlives the operation that started it.
A fast source — a resize, a scroll, a stream — updates state at most once per frame, folding its events in batches.

An operation that may be repeated is idempotent: a key is minted once per intent and sent with every attempt, child identifiers are derived deterministically, and a transition to the current state does nothing.

A pattern answers a present problem, and then the canonical one: strategy plus registry for vendors and kinds, factory or module object for adapters, decorator at the composition root, reducer for transitions, transition table for state machines, builder for test data.
Behaviour is composed from small units.
Don't-repeat-yourself applies to knowledge, not to text that merely looks alike.
A function either answers a question or changes state, never both.
A unit calls its own collaborators, never the collaborators of their collaborators: no chain that walks into another object's internals.
A spec proves one boundary and is named after it.
A constant gets a spec only when a reader outside the code relies on it — a code users script against, a name another system reads — and then as one table per contract.
A case checks an outcome a caller observes — a returned value, a changed state, what a user sees — and a call on a fake only when the call itself is the behaviour.
A case earns its place by failing for a plausible bug no other case catches.
A case proves one intent and asserts it with strict equality on the whole outcome.
Variants of one behaviour are one table of cases, each row naming its condition.
No snapshot of a structure a reader cannot check by eye.
Every failure a boundary declares has a case that produces it and checks what the caller receives.
Edge cases are chosen by risk: empty input, limits, Unicode, invalid input, a concurrent call, a lost connection.
An invariant is proven by a property test where one pays — a value object's guard, an invertible mapper, a reducer — with its cases in the spec of its unit.
A lifecycle test takes an object made by its factory through every transition to its final state, and checks each step.
Each port has one contract suite, run against its fake and against its real adapter.
Tests ship in the same change as the behaviour they prove.
Every test has been seen failing for the right reason: written before the code, or after it with the code broken for a moment.
A bug fix begins with the test that reproduces the bug, seen failing before the fix.
When a behaviour is described before it is built — in an issue or a plan — an agent writes its tests from the description first.
Tests touch no network, no real file system outside a temporary folder, no real clock, no process they did not start and no credential.
Network, time, randomness, processes and credentials are faked through their ports, with one fake per port, named `<port>.fake`.
Each adapter is proven against its real engine inside the sandbox, in `<name>.integration.spec`, with a case for each port operation and each failure it maps.
Each critical scenario `PROJECT.md` names has one end-to-end test through the delivery layer, in `<name>.e2e.spec`.

A file in `__tests__/`, or in the folder of end-to-end specs, is a spec named after the file or scenario it proves — `<name>.spec`, `<name>.integration.spec`, `<name>.e2e.spec` — a fake `<port>.fake`, or fixtures `<name>.fixtures`, and nothing else; the language fixes the spelling.
Production code never imports a file of `__tests__/` or of the end-to-end folder.
A suite is named after its boundary, and a case reads `should <behaviour> when <condition>`, in the language's spelling.
A case has three parts — Arrange, Act, Assert — each marked and present once, and Act makes one call.
No test is skipped, pending, focused or without an assertion.
The project's check runs the tests, and fails when one fails.

All logic — the domain, the adapters, the libraries, the UI — is held at 100 percent of lines and functions, and of branches where the runner measures them, reached only through the tests of its boundaries.
Mutation testing measures the tests, and every mutant of the logic is killed.
No secret is committed — not in code, documents, tests, fixtures or history.
A secret never travels in a URL, and never reaches a build artefact: an image layer, a client bundle, a variable baked in at build time.
A secret that leaked — into a commit, a log, a message — is rotated at once, and the access made with it while it was exposed is checked.
No secret and no personal data appear in logs, errors, test data or documents.
Every environment variable the program reads is declared in one place, and code reads only declared names.
A credential belongs to one identity and one purpose, per environment, with only the permissions its job needs, documented beside its use.
A language uses one package manager, and one lockfile, committed.
A third-party step of CI is pinned to an immutable reference, never to a moving tag or branch.
Dependency updates arrive as pull requests from an update bot, each passing the check before it is merged.
A new release of a dependency is adopted only after a cooldown of some days, except a fix for a known vulnerability.

A new dependency is a decision: it needs a reason it cannot be a few lines of the project's own, and it is checked against the risk signs of a new package — a name one typo from a popular one, younger than thirty days, under a hundred weekly downloads, a recent change of owner, no source repository, obfuscated code.
A dependency deprecated as a whole is replaced — by its successor, another package, or the project's own code.
A dependency's install scripts run only when the dependency is listed by name as allowed to run them.
A high or critical known vulnerability in any dependency, development dependencies included, fails the check.
Every dependency's licence is on the project's allowlist.
Commit hooks, linter configurations and release automation come from shared, pinned packages, not from copies in each repository.
An operation that destroys data, spends money, touches a live system or sends something outward runs only with an explicit flag and a person's go-ahead; its default is to show what it would do.
Access is denied unless a rule grants it.
Before a change, read the rules that govern it: core's chapters and the files of the active blocks whose concern the change touches.
A change does what the task asks and nothing else: no unrelated refactor, reformat or rename.
A file that moves is moved, never deleted and written anew, and a moved file is not rewritten in the same step.
One command runs every check of the repository — format, lint, types, tests, coverage, mutation, the rest of the project's tools — and `constitution.yaml` names it.
The check verifies and never changes a tracked file: it generates nothing, formats nothing and rewrites nothing.
The check passes, with no error and no warning, before a change is reported done.
Before a change is handed back, it is reviewed against every active rule that no tool holds, not only those the task seemed to touch.
A repository keeps at its root `constitution.yaml`, the blocks it follows and their overrides, and `PROJECT.md`, the product's context.
`README.md` says what the repository is, how to install and run it, and how to change it — for a reader who knows nothing else.
`docs/` is for readers outside the code: users, integrators, operators.
Specs, plans and working notes live in a `local/` folder that version control ignores.
Generated files are not committed; the build produces them.
Files and folders are named in kebab-case.
A public repository carries a licence file that names its author.
A rule is never broken silently.

An agent asks before: adding a dependency, a pattern or an abstraction; changing a public surface, a schema or a format; an operation that destroys, costs money, touches a live system or sends something outward; a call to a real external service; pushing to a shared branch.
A design question is settled in the chat before code is written for it.
When a request can be read in two ways that lead to different work, the agent asks.
Outcomes are reported as they are: a failing test with its output, a skipped step as skipped, a claim about the code checked against the code.
Only a person decides what is committed.
An agent never merges, never pushes to the main line, never force-pushes and never rewrites shared history.
Commits, pull requests and documents carry no attribution to the tool or model that helped write them.
An agent that delegates keeps the responsibility: it names the rules and files that govern the task, and checks what comes back before it relies on it.
A sub-agent does the work it is given and nothing more: it never commits, never pushes or merges, never runs a live system and never calls a real external service.
A project keeps no agent instruction file of its own that restates a rule; the constitution delivers the rules, and `PROJECT.md` the context.
What an agent learns about the product goes into `PROJECT.md` through a change a person reviews; an agent's private memory is never the project's fact.

Every interface meets WCAG 2.2 AA — among its criteria, captions and transcripts, resize, reflow and text spacing, at most three flashes a second, a way past repeated blocks, a single-pointer alternative to dragging, a minimum target size, and consistent navigation.
Native semantic elements come first; roles and states are added only where no native element exists, and only correct ones.
Every interactive element works with every input the platform offers — keyboard, pointer, touch, assistive technology.
Focus is always visible, at 3:1 contrast against its background; no focus indicator is removed without the design system's replacement.
Every control and field has an accessible name.
Errors and changes of status are announced: an urgent one interrupts, the rest wait their turn.
Colour never carries meaning alone; a status colour comes with an icon or a word.
Contrast is proven by a test over every pair of semantic foreground and background tokens, in each theme: 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for large text, and 3:1 for controls, borders and focus.
Whatever hover reveals is reachable by focus and by a tap or long press; no action appears only on hover.
When the user asks for reduced motion, motion that is not essential stops.
Headings go in order, and no level is skipped.
Every screen and component spec runs an accessibility scan, and passes with zero violations.
Before a new interactive component ships, a person operates it with the keyboard or a switch, and with a screen reader.
The scanner runs over the rendered tree inside a spec, covers the WCAG 2.2 A and AA rules it can decide, and reports each violation with its element.
Nothing is tracked, and no identifier is stored, before the user consents; declining changes nothing else in the product.
Every event belongs to one closed vocabulary, each with its typed parameters; no free-form name or value is sent.
Each analytics service is one sink, one `.sink` file in `sinks/`, under one contract beside the folder; a registry chooses the active sinks.
A feature never sends an event; the composing layer translates the feature's intents and outcomes into events.
A failing sink neither breaks the user's action nor silences the other sinks; its fault is reported out of band.
No personal data and no content a person wrote is sent in an event.
The project keeps a written list of what is never tracked, and why.
Key product outcomes — a conversion, a reason something was blocked, the use of a feature — have events, so business measures come from analytics.
Context shared by every event — signed in or not, the mode — is set once, as a dimension.
The library sends nothing and stores no identifier until consent allows it.
Addresses are anonymised, and no user identifier is sent unless configured.
The library loads and sends without delaying rendering.
Dimensions set once apply to every later event.
One document the user writes is the program's single input; every run reads it whole, validates it, and moves the world toward it.
Each section of the document has a strict schema: unions selected by a discriminant field, unknown keys rejected, every constraint between fields checked in validation, never at the point of use.
A section may be absent, and is then left untouched.
A secret in the document is a reference by name to the environment.
Each kind of value — a size, a duration — has one syntax in the document, parsed once.
The schema published for editors is generated from the code's schema, never written by hand.
The document and its schema live in `composition/`, which knows every section.
An `init` command writes one document from a template, named after the program, pointing editors at the published schema.
Validate, render, plan and apply are separate use-cases: each runs alone, and later ones reuse earlier ones.
A pipeline use-case keeps its stages under `steps/`, in the order the use-case calls them; a stage never calls another.
The plan names every change that destroys something, and apply refuses one without an explicit flag.
Applying the same document twice reports no change the second time, and a test proves it.
A run reports each stage — skipped with its reason, unchanged, changed, ran, failed — as a value the delivery layer prints.
What a run produces lands in one work folder that version control ignores.
Engines the program drives are not vendored: each is downloaded per release into the program's home, pinned by version and checksum, and reached only through a port.
Developers and CI run exactly the engines the program installed, linked into one directory of its home.
The library offers strict objects that fail on an unknown key.
The library offers unions selected by a discriminant field, with an error that names it.
The library generates a JSON Schema from the code's schema.
Every string a user reads comes from the message catalog, by key; none is written in code.
A message takes its values as named parameters; a sentence is never built by joining strings.
Plural and ordinal forms come from the locale's CLDR rules, inside the message, never from a condition in code such as "the count is one".
The current locale is reachable anywhere in the presentation without being passed as a prop.
Domain and application code return codes and values, and the presentation turns them into text; the message library never reaches the domain.
Numbers, dates, currencies and lists are formatted by the locale.
Plural and ordinal forms are selected by CLDR data.
A message takes named parameters inside it.
A missing or misspelt key fails the check.
Each locale's catalog loads on demand.
A repository of packages keeps each package at `packages/<language>/libs/<name>/`, language-free files and hooks in `packages/common/`, and templates per language and in `common`.
The root of a repository of packages is private: it holds only the workspace, the scripts of the check, and a README with one row per package.
A package holds its manifest, its README, its licence, its `configs/` or `src/`, and its `__tests__/`.
A package is named `<scope>/<kit>-<language>-<name>`, after what it configures.
`common` imports nothing.
A package ships configuration, primitives or tooling, never a product's business, and knows nothing of those who install it.
The manifest lists every entry a consumer may use and nothing else, and names the files it ships.
The tool a package configures is a peer dependency with a lowest supported version, never a dependency of the package.
Consumers extend a package's entries; they never copy its files.
A file no tool can extend is a template: kept canonical under `templates/`, copied once, then owned by the consumer.

A consumer takes a package by the tool's own extends, else by a one-line module that re-exports it, else by the tool's remote configuration; it pins the package through its lockfile and updates it through the bot.
The root of a repository of packages installs its own packages and extends them as a consumer would.
A copy generated from `common` is rebuilt by the package's build, never edited by hand, and a spec asserts it equals its source.
Each shipped configuration has a spec that parses it and asserts its intent; code a package runs is held by the coverage gate like any other.
Every package ships its licence file.
A package's README shows the install line, the one-line extends and its options.
All packages of a repository share one version; two packages at different versions are an error.
Versions follow semantic versioning: major for a breaking change of an entry, shipped with its migration; minor for an addition; patch for a fix.
A deprecated entry names its replacement and the version that removes it.
One tag publishes every public package; a version already published is skipped, so a rerun is safe.
The registry trusts the release job's identity and records provenance; no stored token publishes.
The changelog of a release is the commit subjects since the previous tag, features and fixes first.
The root resolves its own packages from the working tree, not from the registry.
The tool publishes through a CI identity with provenance, without a stored token.
The remote system owns its data: it lives only in the cache of remote data, is never copied into a store, and the program never becomes a second source of it.
Every response is parsed against its wire schema in the adapter before it is mapped, so a change of the wire fails at that one boundary.
One shared mapper turns transport failures into domain errors: it handles unauthorized and unexpected failures itself and takes each feature's map of codes.
Each feature owns one key factory, and every cache key is built through it from the port's parameters, never by hand.
A write invalidates only its own feature's keys.
A progressive result is an asynchronous sequence of domain events the port returns: its end completes it, a domain error fails it, and stopping the loop cancels it.
Events that build an entity are folded by a pure reducer of the domain, and the stream reaches the cache in batches, at most once per frame.
A stream that ends without its terminal event fails with a domain error.
Every read can be cancelled; a read superseded for the same key is cancelled, and only the latest answer reaches the cache.
Where another system owns the data, the program keeps no aggregates, domain events, event sourcing or specifications of its own.
Reads with one key share one request and one entry.
The cache invalidates by a prefix of the key, with or without a refetch.
Reads in flight for a key can be cancelled.
A write has hooks before it runs, on failure and after it settles, with a context for rollback, and the variables of pending writes can be read.
One handler sees every failed read and write.
Staleness and refetching are set per key.
The transport sets a timeout on every request, per call, and cancels a request by signal.
The transport tells a status failure, a network failure and a timeout apart, for the mapper.
Retries are configurable by method and status, with backoff, and off for writes that are not idempotent.
One configured instance — base address, headers, credentials — is built by the composition root and passed to the adapters that need it.
A screen owns its navigation state: it reads and validates it, loads its data or delegates the loading, and composes the page from widgets and pieces private to it.
A presentational component or a screen's piece imports no navigation or route-parameter primitive.
Navigation reaches a presentational component through a slot that renders the link — its children first, then the data; any other action reaches it through a callback.
Pieces and binding units private to one screen live beside it, private to it.
By default the screen loads the data and its pieces render it.
Guards and redirects of a screen live in the screens layer and use the surface of the feature that owns sessions; feature interfaces adapt to permissions passed down by composition.
Every screen sits inside an error boundary that says what happened and what to do next, and one boundary in `root/` catches what the screens do not.
Every data view shows four states: loading, empty, error and content.
An error says what happened and what to do next.
A button names its result, verb and object — never "Submit" or "OK".

Each kind of state has one home: remote data in its cache; view state a link or a restart must reproduce in the platform's navigation state; ephemeral state in its component; the few global concerns — theme, session, notices — in one small store.
A form's schema composes the predicates of the value objects and sits with the form; it never restates an invariant.

A component lives where its knowledge lives: used by one screen, beside it; knows a feature, in that feature's `ui/`; a generic primitive, in `libs/ui`; specific to the application and used by two or more features, in `shared/ui`; the application's shell, in `root/ui`.
A component's folder name carries its location and role: no prefix in `libs/ui` and `shared/ui`, `root-` in `root/ui`, the feature's name in a feature, and `-widget` on every widget.
A component in `components/` takes data and callbacks, performs no input or output, and imports no binding unit.
A feature's `ui/` imports `libs/ui`, `shared/ui`, its own binding units, its entities as types, and `kernel/`; never adapters, contracts or domain use-cases.

A component has its own folder: the component file, its `.types`, `.variants` and `.constants` when it needs them, its sub-components prefixed with its name in `components/`, and a surface offering only its public API.
A need is met by existing components first, then by extending a primitive, and only then by a new primitive that is composed in.
A dialog, popover, menu, combobox, select, tabs, tooltip, accordion and their kin are built on the accessible primitive library, never by hand.
A component installed as source is, before review, placed and named by the homes above, restyled to tokens, stripped of unused props and made to follow the prop rules.
A component with a second region, an optional part or a slot is a compound: a root with named parts, its content passed as children.
The root of a compound owns the choreography of its animated regions and shares it through the compound's context.
A prop passed unchanged through more than two levels calls for composition or a nearer widget, never for a store read in a deep component.
A boolean prop starts with `is` for a state, `has` for content, `with` for an opt-in part, `should` for a policy, or `as` for a polymorphic render; never a bare, mixed or negated name.
A callback prop is named `on<Event>`, and the handler inside the component may be `handle<Event>`.
Before a prop is added, the existing name for the same meaning is reused; synonyms are converged in the change that finds them.
An optional prop no call site uses is deleted, and its default inlined.
The primitive library holds no user-facing text and no message catalog; text arrives through props.
A component sizes to its container, not to the screen.
Drag and drop shows that an item can be grabbed, that it is grabbed, where it can land, and a preview of the result.
Every target meets the platform's minimum size, counting its padding.
A screen's spec proves each data state, each interaction that changes something, each message the user sees and each navigation.
A reusable component's spec proves the variants that change behaviour or meaning, its keyboard use, its focus, and its accessible name, role and state.
A spec finds elements by role, label and text, never by class or internal state.
Appearance is compared by screenshot only where the look is the contract: in the design system.
Complex patterns follow the platform's keyboard conventions; focus moves into a layer, stays in it and returns from it; Escape dismisses it.
Primitives carry no look of their own.
Primitives have no built-in user-facing text.
A slot renders the consumer's element with the primitive's behaviour.
Every visual value — colour, space, size, type, radius, shadow, motion, layer — comes from a token of the theme module, which also holds the theme's constants and modes.
Tokens are named `<namespace>.<group>.<role>[.<step>]`, in four layers: primitive, never used by a component; semantic, on closed vocabularies; common, for the shell's constants; composite.
No token is named after a component; a component's look comes from its variants.
Light and dark are one set of semantic tokens.
A component's variants are one declarative map from variant to style, in its `.variants` file, which also types the variant props.
A variant that restyles descendants is set once on their ancestor and resolved by the styling cascade, never passed down as a prop.
Durations and easings are tokens of two kinds, micro and macro; motion driven from code uses the same tokens, so a request for reduced motion switches them all.
The library's default scales can be reset, and a value outside the tokens is rejected by a check.
One token set resolves both light and dark.
Styles respond to the size of the container.
An ancestor's state restyles its descendants without props.
The variant engine declares the map and derives the types of the variant props from it.
A binding unit that loads or writes returns a union keyed by `status`.

The providers are the application's composition root: they build the configuration, the transport and the cache client, build each adapter by its factory from the transport, and hand the adapters to the binding units.
A binding unit binds one operation: it takes its adapter from the providers and calls the use-case, or the port when there is none.
The configuration provider is the application's one reader of the environment, and parses it once, at boot.
After a write, invalidation happens in the command's binding unit, through the feature's key factory.
An optimistic write happens only in the mutation's lifecycle, which can roll it back, never in the request itself.

Under concurrent writes, reads in flight for the touched keys are cancelled before the snapshot; a failure rolls back only its own changes; invalidation waits until the last write settles; and an item whose identifier the server assigns renders from the pending variables under a stable key.
A request driven by typing is sent after a pause, or on the deferred value.
The cache's global error handler, wired by the providers, turns an unauthorized failure into session state through the surface of the feature that owns sessions.
A screen's spec and a binding unit's spec run inside their providers, with the transport replaced by captured responses.
Every request over the network has a timeout and can be cancelled.
A timeout or a lost connection is an expected, typed failure the user sees and can retry, never a hang or a silent loss.
Input the user entered survives a failed request and is sent again without being typed again.
A request's timeout and its lost connection each have a test case.
Nothing shipped to the client — code, configuration, data in memory or in storage — is treated as hidden from its user.
No secret is in client code, a client bundle or a value built into it.
Every check on the client — validation, permission, limit, price — is repeated where the client cannot reach it.
A commit holds one logical change, and its subject says what changed.
A refactor and a change of behaviour are never one commit.
Every commit passes the repository's check: the commit hooks run its fast part, CI runs all of it.
The reason for a change is written down where the flow puts it, beside the change, not only in a conversation.
Every change reaches the main line through a reviewed pull request.
The main line is protected: no direct push, no force push, no deletion.
The check runs in CI on every pull request, and a red check blocks the merge.
A repository integrates by one strategy, which the protection enforces, and no work-in-progress or fix-up commit reaches the main line.
A pull request is small enough to review in one sitting; one that mixes concerns is split.
A branch is deleted once it is merged.
When work is handed back, the working copy holds no stray change and no scratch file outside ignored folders.
History others have is never rewritten.
A release is marked by a tag of its version on the commit it was built from, and a tag never moves.
Releases are cut by automation from the merged changes; a person promotes a pre-release to a release.
Large binary files live outside the history, stored by reference.
A secret that reached the history is compromised: it is rotated at once, and rewriting the history does not undo the leak.
The program's logic runs in the tab.
Code that can render on a server reads no browser global while it renders.
One bundle serves every environment: its configuration is served beside it and read once, at boot, by the configuration provider.
Each bundle has a size budget the check holds, the embeddable one first.
A message from another window is accepted only from an expected origin, and parsed; an outgoing message names its target origin.
`<button>` for an action, `<a href>` for a move, lists as lists, tables with headers and a caption; ARIA only where HTML has no element.
Every page has landmarks — header, navigation, main, footer — and a link to skip to the content comes first.
A field for the user's own data declares its purpose with `autocomplete`.
A status goes to a polite live region, and only an urgent error to an assertive one.
The focus ring is the design system's, shown on `:focus-visible`; `outline: none` needs that replacement.
Type sizes are in `rem`, text spacing may be overridden by the user, and at 320 CSS pixels content reflows without scrolling sideways.
Before a new interactive component ships: Tab reaches it in visual order, Enter or Space works it, Escape closes a layer, focus returns to its trigger, and a screen reader announces it as it should.
View state a link or a reload must reproduce — filters, sort, page, selection, the open tab — lives in the URL, and nothing else does.
Title, description and links of the document are declared by the screen or component that owns them; a third-party script is declared where it is used.
Navigation renders an anchor with a real `href`, handed to presentational components through their slot.
Base styles serve the smallest screen, and wider screens add overrides from a minimum width; nothing desktop-first is undone.
Heights use dynamic viewport units or the container, never `100vh`, `100vw` or a fixed width in pixels.
A pointer target is at least 24 × 24 CSS pixels, padding included, and 44 for a primary touch target.
A hover style that changes visibility has a state without hover, or sits behind `@media (hover: hover)`.
A variant that restyles descendants is a `data-*` attribute on their ancestor, resolved by the stylesheet.
Content images carry `srcset` and `sizes`, in a modern format; a canvas scales by the device's pixel ratio; icons are SVG.
On a foldable screen, content and controls never cross the fold; the layout follows the viewport segments the browser reports.
The delivery layer is `cli/`: one `<name>.cli` file per command, shared flag definitions in files beside them, reused and never declared twice, and the list of commands registered beside the files.
A command parses its flags, resolves its input, calls one use-case or composition, and prints the result.
What a run reports is a value the command prints at the end, never lines the logic prints along the way.
Data goes to standard output; diagnostics and failures go to standard error.
A command that reports data prints it as JSON when given `--json`.
Exit codes come from one map: 0 success, 1 a failure the user can act on, 2 a usage error — an unknown command, a bad flag — and 70 an internal error, the program's own bug.
Every value the run knows to be secret is masked in all output, an engine's output included, before it is printed.
A setting given in several places takes the flag first, then the environment, then the file.
Without a terminal the program never prompts; a missing answer is a usage error that names its flag.
A command's spec runs the program on an argument list with a fake command context, and checks standard output, standard error and the exit code.
Flags are declared with a schema and parsed before the handler runs.
The program's handler decides every exit code, the framework's own failures included.
The framework's terminal, prompts, clock and process hooks can be replaced in a spec.
View state a deep link or a restart must reproduce lives in the navigation parameters, and a deep link's parameters are parsed like any untrusted input.
Going to the background, being suspended or being ended by the system loses no input and no view state.
Offline, the app opens, shows the data it has cached, marked as such, and says which actions wait.
Permissions, notifications, background work, secure storage and sensors are reached through adapters behind ports, never from a screen.
Tokens and credentials live only in the system's secure storage.
Every interactive element declares its accessible label, role and state through the system's accessibility properties.
The screen reader's order follows the visual order.
Text follows the system's text size, and layouts reflow to fit it.
The system's reduced-motion and increased-contrast settings are honoured.
Before a new interactive component ships, a person operates it with each system's screen reader, and with a switch or a keyboard.
A touch target is at least 44 × 44 points, or 48 × 48 density-independent pixels, padding included.
Content and controls stay inside the safe areas of the screen.
The focused field and its action stay above the on-screen keyboard.
The system's back gesture goes back, and the app's own gestures never fight the navigator's.
An import that leaves its module uses `#/`; files inside one module import each other by relative path.
`#/` is declared in `imports` of `package.json` (`"#/*": "./src/*"`), the source the runtime reads.
Source files are kebab-case `.ts`, and `.tsx` only where markup is written.
A file with one export is named after it — `order-status.ts` exports `OrderStatus`; a file with several exports names the unit they form.
PascalCase for types, classes, enums and their members; camelCase for functions, variables and instances; SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for a constant value, camelCase for a constant object or function.
A type is a noun, undecorated: no `I` prefix, on ports too, and no `Type` or `Interface` suffix.
A group of named values is a string `enum`.
Internal code spells absence as `undefined`: `?: T` for what may be absent, `T | undefined` only where an explicit `undefined` means something, `return;` for no result.
Comparisons are strict — `===` and `!==`, with `null` too; never `==`.
`??` gives a default and `?.` reaches through an absent value; `!value` is never a check for absence on a value that is not boolean.
No `any`: not `: any`, `as any`, `Record<string, any>` or `Promise<any>`, in tests too; `noImplicitAny` is never turned off.
No `as` cast except `as const`, no `!` non-null assertion, no `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-nocheck`.
A value from beyond the boundary — `JSON.parse`, a response body, a file, a message — is `unknown` until a schema parses it.
A branch over a union handles every member: a `switch` whose default proves `never`, or an `if` chain that ends in a `never` check.
Conformance to a type is checked with `satisfies`, which keeps the narrow type, not with `as` or a widening annotation.
An identifier's brand is `string & { readonly __brand: 'OrderId' }` or a unique symbol, set only in the mapper at the boundary.

A project may declare semantic aliases — `type Email = string` — in one ambient `types.d.ts` at its source root: only aliases it uses, each for a meaning found in two or more places, never for a string that is just a string.
A type derivable from an exported parent in one or two indexed accesses is derived where it is used, not exported under a name of its own.
Arguments past the first travel in one options object, typed by an interface named `<Function>Input`.
JSDoc documents only a public API whose use is not obvious, never a self-describing property or parameter.

The compiler, not a bundler or the runtime, is the type gate: `tsc --noEmit` runs in the check with the strict options — `strict`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `noUnusedLocals`, `noUnusedParameters`, `noImplicitOverride`, `noImplicitReturns`, `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`.
Build, test and lint tools are development dependencies, and production code imports none of them.
Each dependency has one version across every manifest of the repository.
A manifest's ranges are caret ranges; the lockfile pins the exact versions.
A package that holds state or types across the program — the schema engine, the interface framework — resolves to one version in the lockfile.
The fields of `package.json` follow the shared order.
`exports` in `package.json` maps each entry to its file, with a `types` condition beside `default` wherever a consumer imports code; `files` lists exactly what ships.
The tool a package configures is a `peerDependencies` entry with a `>=` floor.
The build runs the React Compiler over every component and hook.
No `useMemo`, `useCallback` or `memo`: the Compiler memoises.
Only the modern API: `use(Context)`, `<Context value>`, `ref` as a prop, ref callbacks that return their cleanup, actions.
Components are functions, composed, never inherited; a class only for an error boundary.
Hooks are called only at the top level of a component or a hook, never in a condition, a loop or a callback.
No component is defined inside another component.
A list's key comes from the item's identity, never its index.
A value that can be derived is computed during render, never stored in state and synchronised by an effect.
An effect synchronises with a system outside React — never state from state, never the response to an event.
Every effect cleans up what it starts — subscriptions, listeners, sockets, timers — and aborts its asynchronous work, so only the latest response lands.
A component file calls no effect hook: its effects live in hooks in `<name>.hooks.ts` beside it, and input or output goes only through binding units.

Pending, optimistic and transition state go through `useActionState`, `useTransition` and `useOptimistic`; optimism local to a component is `useOptimistic`, optimism over cached data is the data library's.
A hook that folds a fast source schedules its state once per animation frame; an expensive render driven by input reads `useDeferredValue`.
A compound's parts are attached to its root with a typed `Object.assign`, and the root shares its state — the choreography of animated regions included — through `<name>.context.ts`.
A slot that keeps control of its element takes a `ReactElement`; a container takes `ReactNode`; a render-prop slot is `(children, …data) => ReactElement`.
A screen's error boundary catches the render errors below it, reports once, and shows the screen's error state.
An operation's binding unit is a hook in `<op>.hooks.ts`: it takes its adapter from the providers' context and calls the use-case, or the port when there is none.
The check scans the history the clone holds and the uncommitted changes, staged or not, and CI runs it on every pull request.
The whole history, every ref, is scanned once when the scanner is adopted, and before a first public release.
Every scan passes `--redact`: a report shows a finding by its rule, file and line, never by its value.

A false positive is allowed on its line by `betterleaks:allow` followed by its reason, or by its fingerprint in `.betterleaksignore` under a `#` line that states the reason; never by disabling a rule.
A suppression is `// biome-ignore lint/<group>/<rule>: <reason>`: one rule and its reason; never a range or a whole file without one.
Warnings fail the check: every rule is an error, or the check passes `--error-on-warnings`.
The check runs `biome check` without `--write`; `lint:fix` writes.
A project's own GritQL rule lives in `biome/<name>.grit`, scoped by an override, until a shared preset carries it: devkit's, or the constitution's when the rule names the constitution's folders.
Bun installs (`bun install`), runs scripts (`bun run`) and runs binaries (`bunx`); never npm, yarn, pnpm or npx, except `npm publish` in the release workflow.
CI and every script install with `bun install --frozen-lockfile`.
Bun runs no dependency's install script unless `trustedDependencies` in `package.json` lists that package by name.
`minimumReleaseAge` under `[install]` in `bunfig.toml` sets the cooldown for new releases.
The check runs `bun audit --audit-level=high`, development dependencies included.
`bunfig.toml` sets `[run] bun = true`, so every tool, one with a Node shebang included, runs on the pinned Bun.
Another runtime or tool runs only where Bun cannot run it, with the reason written in the configuration or script that makes the exception.
Bun's automatic loading of the local environment file is off — `--no-env-file` in the entry's shebang and in the scripts — so the program reads its environment only where the configuration is parsed.
Each tool has an `<area>:check` script that only checks, and an `<area>:fix` beside it where the tool can write; `check` chains the check scripts.
A program is built by `bun build`, in CI after the check.
The root `package.json` is `private` and declares `"workspaces": ["packages/<language>/libs/*"]`.
The root installs the repository's own packages as `workspace:*` development dependencies.
The version command writes the version into the root's and every package's manifest.
A case compares with `toStrictEqual`, never `toEqual`.
No `mock.module` and no `spyOn` over a real module: effects are faked through their ports.
The unit run leaves out `*.integration.spec.ts`; integration specs run as their own script of the check.
Each command file exports `create<Name>Command(context)`, which returns `defineCommand({ name, description, options, handler })`; the root builds the context, and `createCLI` registers the commands.
Every flag is `option(schema, { short, description })`, its schema a standard schema, and the handler receives the parsed flags.
Every handler runs its work through the program's one error handler, which maps a failure to the exit map.
A command's spec builds the program with a fake terminal and prompt session — `createCLI(meta, terminal)` — and runs it on an argument list.
The native projects are generated from `app.config.ts` and config plugins, never committed or edited by hand.
Variables with the public prefix are built into the bundle, so none holds a secret.
Tokens and secrets on the device live in the system keychain through secure storage, never in plain asynchronous storage.
Expo Router's root is `src/routes/`, so `app` keeps its meaning as a feature's layer.
Native modules are installed at the versions the SDK supports, and the check verifies them with `expo install --check`.

A commit's header follows Conventional Commits 1.0.0 as `type: Subject`, with one of four types: `feat` adds a feature; `fix` fixes a bug; `refactor` changes structure without changing behaviour; `chore` is everything else that changes no behaviour — dependencies, tooling, documentation, releases.
A commit's body and footer are empty.
The type matches the diff: `feat` adds behaviour, `fix` corrects it, `refactor` and `chore` change none; `!` marks every change a consumer must adapt to.
The subject states what changed, not which files were touched.
Placeholder subjects are rejected: "update", "fix stuff", "wip", "changes", "misc".
A branch is named `feature/`, `fix/` or `hotfix/`, then `<issue>-<kebab-name>`.
The type of the merged branch sets the version bump: `feature` a minor one; `fix`, `hotfix` and dependency updates a patch.
Pull requests are squash-merged; the title becomes the commit's subject and follows the commit format.
CI checks the pull request's title and branch name against the formats, since a local hook can be skipped and the title is typed on the forge.
With staged changes, a file is moved with `git mv`, so the index records a rename.
Files are staged by name or by hunk, never with `git add .` or `-A`, and the staged diff and status are read before the commit.
A worktree holds one branch, and its dependencies are installed in it, never linked from another checkout.
A force push goes only to one's own branch that nobody else has, and always with `--force-with-lease`.
A stash carries a message, and `git clean -n` precedes `git clean -fd`.
`.gitignore` covers dependencies, build output, coverage, logs, caches, temporary and backup files, the files of the operating system and of personal editors, and `/local/`.

`.gitignore` covers key and credential files and every local environment file except its example — `.env*` but `.env.example`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.jks`, `credentials.json`, `id_rsa`, `*.secrets`, `.htpasswd` — in nested ignore files too.
A release tag is annotated and named `v<major>.<minor>.<patch>`.
A file over 1 MB goes to Git LFS, or out of the repository.
The check runs knip twice: over everything, and in production mode (`--production`), so code and dependencies that only specs reach count as unused.

One ky instance per remote system is built by the composition root from the configuration — prefix, credentials, headers — and passed to the adapters' factories; no adapter imports it or uses ky's default export.
A response body is read as `unknown` and parsed by the adapter's model schema; `.json<T>()` is a cast and is forbidden.
`HTTPError`, `TimeoutError` and network failures are mapped to domain errors in the adapter, through the shared mapper; nothing of ky crosses the adapter.
ky's timeout stays on, its retries stay on idempotent methods and transient statuses, and the caller's abort signal is passed through.
The hooks come from the shared preset, pinned, never from scripts copied into the repository.
Installing the repository's dependencies installs the hooks, so no clone commits without them.
No commit skips the hooks — no `--no-verify`, no `LEFTHOOK=0` — except the release automation's version commit.
A hook that formats rewrites only the staged files and stages them again; the check itself never writes.
`pre-commit` scans the staged changes for secrets.
Text goes through Lingui's macros — `t`, `<Trans>`, `msg`, `<Plural>` — as ICU messages; never concatenation or an id built by hand.
The check compiles the catalogs in strict mode, failing on a missing translation, and writes no tracked file.
Lingui's command line extracts and compiles the catalogs under Bun; a step that fails there runs under Node from its package script, with the reason written beside it.
The configuration is `.ls-lint.yaml`, passed with `--config`.
Only the Matomo sink knows Matomo — its data layer, and the container's address taken from configuration.
`requireConsent` is set before the first push, and tracking starts only on the consent the user gave.
Tracked URLs carry no identifiers or query values, custom dimensions carry no personal data, and the instance anonymises addresses.
Every tool outside the package manager — the runtime, the package manager itself, other languages' linters — is pinned exactly in `mise.toml`, with `mise.lock` committed and `locked = true`.
CI installs the toolchain from `mise.toml`, so the check runs on the pinned versions, never on the runner's.

A tool outside the package manager takes its shared configuration from devkit's release archive: mise installs `devkit.tar.gz` through its `http` backend, pinned by version and by `checksum`, with `strip_components = 0` so the archive keeps its folders, and a `postinstall` hook links it as `.devkit`, which version control ignores.
`[env] _.path` in `mise.toml` puts the program's engine directory on the PATH for developers and CI; engine versions live in the program, not in `mise.toml`.
`<title>`, `<meta>` and `<link>` are rendered by the component or route that owns them; no head library, and no effect writing to the document head.
A third-party script is rendered as `<script async src>` where it is needed; no script tag is inserted by hand.
ARIA attributes are written hyphenated, as the DOM spells them; the camelCase form is forbidden.
A label names its control with `htmlFor`, and the id comes from `useId`, never typed by hand or random.
An overlay — a dialog, a popover, a toast — renders through a portal.
Browser APIs are read in a hook's effect, or through `useSyncExternalStore` with a server snapshot, never during render.
No raw HTML is injected; untrusted markup goes through a sanitising renderer.
A list that can grow renders through a virtualised list, never `map` inside a scroll view.
React Native is imported only from its package entry, never from its internal paths.
`renovate.json` extends the fleet's preset, pinned to a release.
Update commits and titles follow the commit format: `chore: Update …`, no scope, sentence case.
Minor and patch updates are grouped in one pull request, one per major update, on a schedule, with lockfile maintenance.
A minimum release age of some days holds back every update except a fix for a vulnerability.
Dependency ranges are bumped; a peer range is widened, so its floor stays.
The bot updates the pinned toolchain in `mise.toml` like any dependency.
A dialog, popover, menu, select, combobox, tabs, tooltip, accordion and their kin are built on Radix, directly or through shadcn source.

shadcn source is added with its CLI into the UI kit, after the kit is searched for an equivalent — never imported from a package — and adapted before review: placed and named, restyled to tokens, stripped of unused props, its props conformed, its imports rewritten to the project's alias.
A polymorphic render is Radix's `Slot` behind `asChild`, the only `as` prop.
Every UI-kit component has `<name>.stories.tsx` beside it, with a story per variant and state — disabled, loading, error, empty, long text, both themes.
Stories render from fixtures and fakes; no request leaves a story.
Production code never imports a story, and stories are outside coverage.
Screenshots are compared over the UI kit's stories, where the look is the contract, and nowhere else.
An equivalent mutant is marked on its line — `// Stryker disable next-line <mutator>: <reason>` — one mutator and its reason; never `all`, and never a disable for a whole file.
Stryker drives the specs through its command runner — `bun --config=./bunfig.mutation.toml test --bail` — with coverage off, the end-to-end specs left out, and `coverageAnalysis: "off"`.
Stryker itself runs on Node — its code generator fails under Bun — so the script removes Bun's `node` shim from the PATH.
The check runs `syncpack lint` and `syncpack format --check`.
`@theme` defines only the design system's tokens and resets Tailwind's default scales, so a utility exists only for a token.
A utility with no token behind it — `flex`, `items-center`, `truncate` — is used only where a token would make no sense.
A component's own variants are one `cva` map in `<name>.variants.ts`, which types the props through `VariantProps`.
A cascading variant is a `data-*` attribute on the root, resolved by an `@utility` rule, and never passed down as a prop.
Base classes serve small screens and are widened by `md:`, `lg:` and `xl:`; `max-*:` is forbidden.
Viewport heights use the dynamic units (`h-dvh`), never `h-screen`.
Dark mode redefines the semantic tokens under one selector; a component writes `dark:` only where no token can say it.
Focus is shown by the design system's `focusable` utility, and only it removes an outline.
The motion tokens collapse under reduced motion, in the theme.
Font-size and line-height tokens are in `rem`.
Values, errors, touched and submitting state live in the form instance, with no state per field beside it.
The form validates by a schema beside it, composed from the value objects' predicates, and maps the server's typed error onto its fields.
Submission calls the command's binding unit or an `on<Event>` callback; the form does no input or output, and its submit is disabled while it submits.
A submission that must not repeat creates its idempotency key once, with the form, and reuses it on every retry — never a new key per click.
A read's binding unit wraps `useQuery`, a write's `useMutation`; `queryFn` and `mutationFn` call the adapter the providers hand to the binding unit.
The binding unit returns a union by `status` — pending; error, with its typed error; success, with its data.
Every key comes from the feature's key factory in `app/utils/cache.utils.ts`, built from the port's parameters; no key array is written inline.
Server data lives only in the cache: never copied into state, a context or a store.
A write invalidates its own feature's keys, in `onSettled`; a refresh across features is composed above, or left to staleness.

Optimism lives in the mutation's lifecycle: `onMutate` cancels the reads in flight, snapshots, and writes with domain factories; `onError` restores; `onSettled` invalidates once the last mutation on the key settles; an item whose identifier the server assigns renders from the pending variables instead of a cache write.
`onError` of the `QueryCache` and the `MutationCache`, set where the providers build the client, turns an unauthorized error into session state through the auth feature's surface, once.
The client's `retry` is a predicate on the error's transience, with a limit — never the default three retries on every error; a mutation retries only when it is idempotent.
`queryFn` passes Query's abort signal to the port, so a screen that is left cancels its read.
A stream is folded into the cache with the domain's reducer, in batches of at most one per frame.
A query driven by typing is keyed on the debounced or deferred value, and keeps the previous result as its placeholder.
One `QueryClient` is built where the providers build the rest; each spec builds a fresh client with retries off, inside the providers, with the transport replaced by captured responses.
Screens are file routes under `routes/`; `routeTree.gen.ts` is generated and never edited; `router.tsx` creates the router.
A route owns its URL: it reads and validates its search, runs its loader, and composes the page.
Router primitives — `Link`, `useNavigate`, `useSearch`, `useParams` — are imported only by route files, their private hooks and widgets.
Every route with search parameters validates them by a schema in `validateSearch`.
A write to the search merges with the current parameters, never replaces them.
A screen's private pieces live beside its route in `-components/`, and its private binding units in `-hooks/`.
A layout is a pathless `_name/route.tsx` that renders `<Outlet/>`, never an `index.tsx`.
Access control sits in `beforeLoad`, through a feature's composition outside React, and ends in `redirect`.
Each route that loads data declares its error component; the root declares the not-found one.
A route declares its document metadata in `head`, and the root renders `<HeadContent/>`.
Loaders and guards read through the query cache — `ensureQueryData` with the feature's key factory — and the router's own cache is off (`defaultPreloadStaleTime: 0`).
The query client reaches loaders and guards through the router's context, never by importing `root/`.
The application runs in SPA mode: the root route renders on the client, and there is no server function, server route or data access, except the one configuration function below.
One server function reads the environment, parses it by a schema and serves it; the root route loads it once, before anything reads configuration.
The root route is the delivery layer's wiring: it builds the shell — `<HeadContent/>`, `<Scripts/>`, the document's language — and mounts the providers of `root/`.
Hashed assets are served as immutable; the HTML, the runtime configuration and the embed entries are revalidated.
Elements are queried by role first, then by label and text; `getByTestId`, `container.querySelector` and class selectors are forbidden.
Interactions go through `userEvent`, never `fireEvent`.
What appears asynchronously is awaited with `findBy…` or `waitFor`, never a fixed sleep.
A binding unit is proven through the screen or widget that uses it; `renderHook` only for a hook that is a boundary of its own, such as a UI-kit hook.
One render helper in `__tests__/<name>.fixtures` mounts the providers a spec needs, fresh for each spec, with the transport replaced by captured responses.
Every screen and component spec runs the axe scan over what it rendered, and passes with zero violations.
The build does not check types: the check runs the compiler before the build.
Only variables with the public prefix reach the bundle, and each of them is public: none holds a secret.
One build serves every environment: settings per environment are read at run time, never built in through `import.meta.env`; build values only carry facts of the build itself.
The build's output is measured against the bundle's size budget in the check, entry by entry.
The runner picks up exactly `__tests__/**/<name>.spec.*`; integration specs run as a step of their own, and a run that finds no spec fails.
Coverage counts every source file, tested or not, at 100 percent of lines, functions and branches, excluding exactly core's list and the stories.
Interface specs run in a simulated DOM, which is their sandbox; a request no captured response answers fails the case, and time is faked where it matters.
No `vi.mock` of the project's own modules: effects are faked through their ports, and a spy is asserted only when the call is the behaviour.
Mocks, stubbed globals and the environment are restored after every case, and cases pass in any order.
The `yaml` package is imported only by the adapter or the `libs/` wrapper that parses, and its result is `unknown` until a schema parses it.
Every failure of `parse` — a syntax error, and an alias without its anchor, which throws a `ReferenceError` — becomes one coded error with its cause.
YAML is written with `lineWidth: 0`, so no value is folded across lines.
The document's first line is `# yaml-language-server: $schema=<published schema URL>`.
The check runs `yamllint --strict .` over every YAML file; the configuration is `.yamllint.yaml`, extending devkit's template.
zod is imported only at the edge — adapters and their `models/`, the delivery layer's flags, the root's configuration, the document in `composition/` — never under `domain/`.
A schema over a domain type is held to it exactly — `conformingTo<Model>()(schema)`, or `z.ZodType<Model>` where assignability is enough — and an enum's schema is `z.enum(TheEnum)`.
A document the program owns is parsed with `z.strictObject`; a vendor's response with `z.object`, so a new field from the vendor is ignored, not fatal.
`safeParse` runs at the edge, and each issue becomes a detail of one coded error, with its path.
The published JSON Schema is built by `z.toJSONSchema` from the document's schema.
